extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato / readers of classical political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts and commentary from Plato's Republic (Books V–VI) outlining proposals for the ideal state, the education and character of guardians and philosophers, social/sexual/communal regulations, and the epistemological schema (sun/line/dialectic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and communal arrangement of guardians' households
rubrics_metrics.description: After selection the men and women shall dwell in common houses, have their meals in common, and be brought together by regulated festivals and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers select men and women as guardians; they live communally to prevent private interests and produce unity. Marriages are to be organized by the state rather than private choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulated marriage festivals and managed mating
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy marriage festivals will be instituted; rulers will contrive by lots that the brave and the fair come together, and those of inferior breed are paired with inferiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers may manipulate lots and use stratagems so citizens ascribe pairings to chance. Festivals' holiness is tied to usefulness, and mating is managed like animal breeding to improve the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eugenic rearing policy (rearing and disposal of offspring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offspring of the brave and fair will be reared in an enclosure attended by suitable nurses; the rest will be hurried away to places unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children are to be separated from their biological recognition (mothers must not recognize their own offspring), with hired nurses and attendants taking on nursing and night-watching duties to ensure communal child-rearing and control of population quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age limits for permitted parenthood and marital participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents ought to be in the prime of life: for a man thirty years (from twenty-five to fifty-five), and for a woman from twenty to forty; those outside these ages who partake in the hymeneals are guilty of impiety unless rulers consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict age ranges regulate who may participate in state-arranged unions; after these ages persons may range at will, subject to prohibitions against certain degrees of kinship unless dispensation is granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of kinship within the communal system
rubrics_metrics.description: Brothers and sisters are those born seven or nine months after the espousals; parents are those espoused at those times—everyone will have many children and many parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The communal arrangement requires redefinition of familial ties based on timing of public espousals, replacing private lineage with state-defined affinity to maintain social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal property as means to political unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens will have all things in common; in having common property they will have common pleasures and pains—this unity prevents strife, lawsuits, flattery of the rich, and sordid household cares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private property and private interests are identified as sources of discord; communal ownership aligns individual fortunes and sensitivities with the whole State, producing moral and political unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military adaptation of communal principles and training of youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Communism is adapted to military service: parents take children to look on at battles; young warriors must be taught and placed under experienced veterans and taught to ride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training by exposure and apprenticeship (analogous to potters’ boys learning the wheel) conditions bravery; youths should be trained but shielded from unnecessary danger, and given suitable mounts for flight/escape where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of cowardice, desertion, and heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowards and deserters shall be degraded to husbandmen; gentlemen who allow themselves to be taken prisoners may be presented to the enemy; heroes shall be crowned, receive fellowship, kisses, more wives, better seats and meats, and honoured after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state institutionalizes rewards and punishments to shape military virtue: degradation to lower classes for cowardice, public honors and material privileges for bravery, and cultic worship/burial honors for fallen benefactors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and ethics of warfare between kin and against barbarians
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellenes should not be enslaved nor their dead despoiled; there should be limits to devastation—no burning houses nor carrying off more than the annual produce; war between Hellenes is civil and aimed at reconciliation, whereas foreign war differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War among fellow Greeks is treated as family discord and should aim at chastening and reconciliation, not total subjugation or plunder; excessive cruelty or sacrilege (offering Hellenic arms in temples) is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controlled falsehoods by rulers (noble falsehoods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must be skillful physicians of the State, for they will often need a strong dose of falsehood in order to bring about desirable unions between their subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly permits rulers to employ deceit as a social tool to manage population, pairings, and perceptions—an instrument of governance to maintain order and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of licentiousness via state-sanctioned marriage practices
rubrics_metrics.description: They cannot be allowed to live in licentiousness; holy marriage festivals will be instituted; anyone forming a marriage connection outside consent of rulers is guilty of impiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual behavior and timing of unions are regulated morally and legally by the state, with religious sanctification (holiness proportional to usefulness) used to enforce conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers as ideal rulers and their defining qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers should be chosen as rulers if they have other qualities required: lovers of the knowledge of the eternal and of all truth; haters of falsehood; meaner desires absorbed in knowledge; social and gracious disposition; free from cowardice and arrogance; learn and remember easily; harmonious, well-regulated minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosopher's love of universal knowledge, contempt for falsehood, and moral excellence make him fit to rule; these traits are described as rare and difficult to find combined in one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of corruption and the rarity of true philosophers
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher is a rare being and many causes (public opinion, sophists, flattery, exile or death, vulgar ambitions) tend to destroy or corrupt philosophers; public opinion acts as a pervasive Sophist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even people with philosophical tendencies are liable to corruption by politics, fame, or social pressures; this supports the argument for requiring philosophers to be compelled or obliged to hold office to realize the ideal polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and content of guardian/philosophical education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should begin with gymnastics in youth, increasing the gymnastics of the soul as the man strengthens, and when active life is over he should finally return to philosophy; dialectic must be mastered—the present mode of brief, intermittent study is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structured educational regimen: physical training in youth, progressive intellectual cultivation, and a culminating period of dialectic later in life. The true difficulty is learning dialectic rather than fragments of philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing guardians in pleasures, pains, and higher knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians are to be tested in the refiner’s fire of pleasures and pains; aspirants must be tested in pleasures and dangers and in the highest branches of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral testing in adverse circumstances is necessary to reveal steadfastness; intellectual testing up to the highest principles (including understanding the idea of the Good) is also required to qualify guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the idea of the Good as essential leadership competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must understand the supreme principle—the idea of the Good—which is the cause of knowledge and truth; without knowledge of the Good no man has any real knowledge of anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical grasp of the Good is portrayed as the ultimate competence for rulers; it is compared to the sun as the source of light and growth for visible/intelligible worlds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological schema: visible vs intelligible and stages of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Two corresponding worlds—the visible and the intelligible—are represented by the sun and the idea of the Good; a divided line subdividing visible (shadows/reflections, real objects) and intelligible (mathematics, dialectic) marks stages of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics occupies an intelligible-but-descending segment that uses hypotheses; dialectic uses hypotheses to ascend to the idea of the Good and then descends. The schema prescribes cognitive stages for education and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as love of universal knowledge, distinct from lovers of mere opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher loves knowledge of abstract ideas (justice, beauty, good) and has insatiable curiosity; lovers of sights and sounds or those satisfied with opinions are imitators, not true philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True philosophic pursuit seeks the immutable forms, not sensory multiplicity or mere rhetorical disputation; the distinction underscores the temperament and aims required in rulers and guardians.
